 TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:

           COME NOW, Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (“Oncor”) and LCRA Transmission

Services Corporation (“LCRA TSC” and together with Oncor, the “Applicants”) and file this

Reply Brief (“Brief”) regarding the Applicants’ application (“Application”) to amend their

certificates of convenience and necessity (“CCNs”) for the proposed Bell County East Switch to

Big Hill Substation 765 kilovolt (“kV”) transmission line project in Bell, Burnet, Concho, Coryell,

Lampasas, Llano, Mason, McCulloch, Menard, Milam, Mills, San Saba, Schleicher, Tom Green,

and Williamson counties, Texas (the “Project”). As required by State Office of Administrative

Hearings (“SOAH”) Order Nos. 6 and 32, this Brief is timely filed on or before June 26, 2026. 1

                                   I.     REPLY REGARDING NOTICE

           As discussed in detail in Applicants’ initial post-hearing brief, Applicants fully complied

Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) § 22.52(a). 3

           a.    Public-Meeting Notice – 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(4)

would be entitled to receive direct mail notice of the application and must mail notice of that

meeting to landowners within 500 feet of the centerline. 4 The record evidence indisputably

demonstrates Applicants’ compliance with the rule.             The record additionally reflects that

          b.    Application Notice – 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3)

be directly affected. 19 Pursuant to the rule, proof of notice may be established through an affidavit

the current county tax rolls. 20 Upon filing of such proof of mailed notice, the alleged lack of actual,

received notice of any individual landowner will not in and of itself support a finding that the

requirements of the rule have not been satisfied. 21

                     i. Burnet County Commissioners Court

           The Burnet County Commissioners Court (“BCCC”) argues that Applicants did not

provide sufficient notice of the application, emphasizing the requirement to use current county tax

rolls. 31 The record evidence reflects otherwise. Applicants collected land-use data for the 122

alternative routes filed with the Application through a continuous process that began in December

2024 and continued through the filing of the Application in March 2026. 32 Throughout that period,

Applicants utilized county tax rolls in compliance with Commission rules. 33 When Applicants

became aware of a newly affected landowner whose property was not accurately reflected on the

tax rolls, they promptly mailed notice advising the landowner of 15 days from receipt to intervene,

consistent with the process described in Applicants’ Supplemental Notice. 34 Applicants complied

with the requirement to provide notice based on the current tax rolls of each affected county in

accordance with 16 TAC § 22.52(a)(3).

                    ii. Colorado River Alliance

the Commission could approve routes composed of link combinations other than the routes “filed”

                                  II.     REPLY REGARDING PROJECT NEED

          a. Generation Is Not a Viable Alternative to the Project

          Numerous intervenors, including American Stewards of Liberty (“ASL”), Ms. Judy Graci,

the Thomas F. and Heidi A. Green Living Trust (the “Green Trust”), Dos Brothers LLC, the

BCCC, and NF5 Family Limited Partnership (“NF5”) argue that local generation in the Permian

Basin could reduce or eliminate the need for the Project and should have been evaluated as an

alternative to Import Path 2. 44 These arguments fail for several reasons. First, H.B. 5066 does not

contemplate a generation solution.             Second, ordering the development and construction of

generation facilities is outside the Commission’s and ERCOT’s authority. Third, generation

cannot meet the reliability needs of the Permian Basin transmission system.

          H.B. 5066 did not contemplate or authorize a generation solution to meet the reliability

needs of the Permian Basin, which is evident from even a cursory reading of the bill. 45 The title

of H.B. 5066 is “An Act Relating to Electricity Service in Areas of This State with a Need for

Transmission Projects.” 46 The Legislature’s bill analysis explained the legislation was “intended

to spur a bolder, more proactive approach that better syncs transmission planning and

construction process with the dynamic needs of Texas customers.” 47                         H.B. 5066 expressly

designates the Permian Basin as a region “in which transmission capacity is insufficient” 48 and

required ERCOT—the entity responsible for transmission planning, access, and reliability—to

resources have been found; (2) address increasing available capacity to meet forecasted load; and

(3) provide available infrastructure to reduce interconnection times in areas without access to

transmission service.” 49 To meet these objectives, it amended two provisions of PURA that

govern proceedings for transmission CCNs. Those amendments require the Commission—the

Commission to “develop a plan to implement [the Permian Basin Reliability Plan] to ensure timely

development and approval of necessary transmission service improvements.” 50

           It is no accident that H.B. 5066 contains a dozen references to transmission and no mention

of generation. This is an implicit recognition of the Commission’s and ERCOT’s respective roles

under the regulatory framework established in PURA Chapter 39. The Commission has regulatory

authority over transmission and distribution service but not over the production or sale of

electricity, which are governed “by customer choices and the normal forces of competition.” 51

Even where the Commission retains limited authority over generation—for example, to address

abuses of market power among competitive generators or the need for more electricity to serve the

State’s power markets—the Commission is empowered to address those issues by ordering the

construction of additional transmission or distribution facilities, but not new generation. 52

           Similarly, ERCOT serves various functions related to the generator interconnection

process, generation dispatch, wholesale transactions, and reliability standards applicable to

Even with this generation capacity added to the planning models, ERCOT “strongly

recommend[ed]” the 765 kV import paths. 55

regulatory authority and are wholly dependent on the economic motivations of power generation

companies. Arguments that a generation alternative should have been studied are, therefore,

completely baseless. No party making those arguments has pointed to a case in which an

           While the Commission and ERCOT cannot order new generation facilities to be built, the

Legislature took other measures to spur the development of generation in ERCOT. Alongside

H.B. 5066, the 88th Texas Legislature enacted Senate Bill (“S.B.”) 2627, which established the

Texas Energy Fund (“TEF”) to incentivize the construction of new dispatchable generation

are specifically tailored to the competitive generation market and its reliance on competition and

private economic interests. Reading the two pieces of legislation side-by-side underscores that the

Legislature created two separate tools to serve distinct purposes: H.B. 5066 requires new

transmission infrastructure, and S.B. 2627 seeks to incentivize construction of new generation.

Transmission Constraint (“GTC”) that restricts power flows out of the Permian Basin region,

resulting in significant curtailment of generation capacity in West Texas. 58       Moreover, as

           Other alternatives suggested by intervenors are either not viable, are already being

implemented in other contexts, or were evaluated and rejected. For example, intervenors Tom and

Heidi Green complain that high voltage direct current (HVDC) infrastructure was not evaluated as

arrangements instead of taking service from the grid or refuse to provide transmission service when

requested by a customer with a behind-the-meter arrangement. Thus, these arrangements often

reduce an existing generator’s grid output without meaningfully reducing the need for new

transmission infrastructure.
